podcast.title: Hiring Milt Gabler (1941)
podcast.body: Decca Records hired Milt Gabler as a staff producer in 1941, capitalizing on his success with "Strange Fruit." He went on to produce many significant records for the label throughout the 1940s. "Milt Gabler was headhunted away from his own label and became a staff producer at Decker Records in 1941."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 4: "Choo Choo Ch'Boogie" by Louis Jordan

podcast.title: Major Label in Nashville (1956)
podcast.body: In January 1956, when Buddy Holly signed with them, Decca Records in Nashville was considered one of the biggest record labels in the United States. "Decker Records in Nashville, which was at the time one of the biggest record labels in the country."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Rejection of The Beatles (Pre-1964)
podcast.body: Decca famously rejected The Beatles, believing "guitar groups were on the way out" and that the band had "no future in show business." "A band famously rejected by at least one record label, Deca, because they felt that guitar groups were on the way out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Request for William Shatner Album (1968)
podcast.body: Decca Records approached William Shatner, then a young actor gaining success from Star Trek, to record an album. This request led to Shatner creating "The Transformed Man" in 1968. "Well, Deca asked me to make an album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stop Me If You've Heard This One Before

podcast.title: Brief Contract with The Shirelles
podcast.body: Decca Records picked up The Shirelles' song "I Met Him On A Sunday" after its minor local success, buying the group's contract from Florence Greenberg. Although the song charted at number 50, Decca dropped the group after two subsequent singles failed to achieve success. "I met him on a Sunday was a minor local success and was picked up by Deca Records who bought the girls contract out from Greenberg."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 89: "Will You Love Me Tomorrow?" by the Shirelles

podcast.title: Copyright Holder for "The Rolling Stones Songbook"
podcast.body: Decca Records held the copyright for "The Rolling Stones Songbook," an album released in 1966 by The Andrew Loog Oldham Orchestra. The Verve initially negotiated with Decca to license a six-second string figure from this album for their song "Bittersweet Symphony," but Decca did not hold all the necessary rights to The Rolling Stones' catalog, leading to further legal complications. "He then had his people at the record label negotiate with Decker Records, the holder of the copyright of the Rolling Stones songbook, to use those six seconds as a sample."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Unfortunate Sonic Coincidences: The Lawsuits

podcast.title: Dominant Market Share (Early 1960s)
podcast.body: In the early 1960s, Decca and EMI together controlled approximately 85% of the British record market, effectively constituting the entire record industry at the time. "EMI and Decker between them had something like 85% of the market, and basically were the record industry in Britain at the time."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Early Large Label
podcast.body: Decca is mentioned as one of the bigger record labels in the early days when all labels were considered "Indie" before industry consolidation led to the rise of only a few major players. "They were some that were bigger than others like Deca and London and RCA and EMI, but there were literally thousands of small labels that did their own thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: First Recording Home for Wanda Jackson
podcast.body: After being passed over by Capitol Records due to her age, Wanda Jackson was signed to Decca Records. She made her first recordings there with members of Hank Thompson's band. Her first single, a duet with Billy Gray, became a top 10 country hit. However, subsequent solo recordings were less successful, leading to her dissatisfaction and eventual departure from the label when her contract was up.

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 43: "I Gotta Know" by Wanda Jackson

podcast.title: Gender Discrimination Policy
podcast.body: Decca Records, a prominent record label of its era, maintained a discriminatory company policy that barred women from being hired in engineering or sound production roles. Women were only considered for positions such as cleaners or assistants, illustrating significant gender bias in the music industry at the time. "por política de empresa en deca recorso no contrataban a mujeres ni en ingeniería ni en producción de sonidos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Cómo una mujer inventó la música electrónica ⧸ Delia Derbyshire

podcast.title: Hiring Shell Tauhmey for Production
podcast.body: Dick Rowe, A&R at Decca, hired Shell Tauhmey as an independent contractor to produce records for the label. This hiring occurred despite (or perhaps because of) Tauhmey's presentation of "fake" production credits for Capitol Records artists like The Beach Boys and Lou Rawls, possibly because Rowe was eager for anyone with American recording studio experience. "Rowe hired him to produce records for Decker as an independent contractor, and Tauhmey started producing hits like Charmaine by the bachelor's."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 119: "You Really Got Me" by the Kinks

podcast.title: Rejection of The Beatles (Early 1960s)
podcast.body: Decca Records famously rejected The Beatles in the early 1960s. The label's talent scouts expressed the belief that "guitar groups were on their way out," making this a notable historical misjudgment in music industry history. "At around the same time, the Beatles were rejected by Decker Records because their talent scouts believe that guitar groups were on their way out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The More Things Change Part 2

podcast.title: Rejection of The Kinks
podcast.body: Decca Records, under Dick Rowe, turned down the opportunity to sign The Ravens (The Kinks), a decision noted for demonstrating "the same judgement he had shown over the Beatles," famously rejecting both future legendary bands. "Rowe, showing the same judgement he had shown over the Beatles, turned down the opportunity to sign the Ravens to Decker."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 119: "You Really Got Me" by the Kinks

podcast.title: Signed Tommy Steele
podcast.body: Decca Records signed Tommy Steele, with producer Hugh Mendel being particularly eager to secure him, leading to an unusual audition location. "Steele was signed by Decker Records, where Hugh Mendel, the producer of Rock Island Line, was so eager to sign him that he didn't check if any studios were free for his audition."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 48: "Rock With the Caveman" by Tommy Steele

podcast.title: Signing of Buddy Holly and the Crickets
podcast.body: Bob Thiel, who was instrumental in signing Jackie Wilson, had previously signed Buddy Holly and the Crickets to Decca Records. "Bob Thiel at Decker records, who had just signed Buddy Holly and the cricket, to sign Wilson."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Signing of Jackie Wilson
podcast.body: Bob Thiel at Decca Records was persuaded to sign Jackie Wilson, not solely for Wilson's talent, but because his manager Al Green promised he could also sign LaVern Baker when her Atlantic contract expired. "Al Green took on Wilson's management, and managed to persuade Bob Thiel at Decker records, who had just signed Buddy Holly and the cricket, to sign Wilson."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-Four: "Reet Petite" by Jackie Wilson

podcast.title: Signing of William Shatner
podcast.body: Decca Records approached William Shatner, then a young actor experiencing success with *Star Trek*, to make an album in 1968. This invitation led to *The Transformed Man*, Shatner's debut musical work, which explored linking literature with music. "Well, Deca asked me to make an album. I'm a young actor. I'm getting him having some success in the Star Trek."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Outsider Music

podcast.title: The Animals' New Label
podcast.body: After their departure from Mickey Most due to artistic differences, The Animals signed with Decca Records and began working with producer Tom Wilson. "They signed to a new label, Decker, and got a new producer, Tom Wilson"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 115: "House of the Rising Sun" by the Animals

podcast.title: The King Bees Promotion
podcast.body: Decca Records promoted "Liza Jane," the only single released by Davy Jones with The King Bees. Despite the backing of a major label, the single sold poorly, leading Jones to leave the band after only a few weeks. "Though promoted by major label Deca Records, Liza Jane sold poorly, and Jones left after a few weeks to join a new combo, the Manish Boys."

podcast.title: Understanding Changing Music Business
podcast.body: Of all the major labels, Decca was notable for genuinely understanding the evolving music business, leading them to acquire specialty jazz label founders like Milt Gabler and Bob Thiele. "Decker, which of all the major labels was the only one that really understood the way that the music business was changing."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
